check-your-understanding-why-order-matte.title: Check Your Understanding: Why Order Matters

questions.question: A student writes `fac n = n * fac (n - 1)` before `fac 0 = 1`. What happens when they call `fac 0`?
options: It returns `1`, because Haskell checks all the equations and picks the most specific match
It never terminates, because the variable pattern `n` matches `0` first and the base case underneath it is never tried
GHC refuses to compile, reporting overlapping patterns
It returns `0`, because `n` is bound to `0` in the first equation
questions.explanation: Haskell matches equations top to bottom, using the first one that fits — not the most specific one. The pattern `n` matches literally any `Integer`, including `0`, so the first equation always fires, producing `0 * fac (-1)`, then `fac (-2)`, moving away from any base case forever.
optionFeedback: Haskell does not search for the 'most specific' equation — it takes the first equation that matches, top to bottom. That top-to-bottom rule is exactly why the ordering matters here.
Right: the variable pattern `n` swallows `0` before the literal base case gets a chance to match, so the base case underneath it is unreachable.
This compiles without complaint. An unreachable equation is a semantic problem, not a syntax error GHC rejects — the program compiles and then loops.
The first equation does run with `n` bound to `0`, but it does not return `0` directly — it evaluates `0 * fac (-1)`, which recurses further instead of stopping.

questions.question: A function has one base case matching only `n = 0` and a recursive step for every other `n`. Which order is safe?
options: Base case first, recursive step second
Recursive step first, base case second
Order never matters for Haskell function equations
It depends on whether the function uses `Int` or `Integer`
questions.explanation: List the most specific pattern — the literal base case — before the general variable pattern that would otherwise capture it. This is the same most-specific-first rule Chapter 4 gives for writing any multi-equation function.
optionFeedback: Correct — the literal pattern must come first so it gets a chance to match before the general pattern captures everything.
That ordering is exactly the broken version from the previous question — the general pattern shadows the base case and the function never terminates.
Order matters a great deal for the equations of a single function; Haskell always tries them top to bottom and commits to the first match.
`Int` and `Integer` are both matched by a literal pattern the same way; the type does not change which equation is tried first.

check-your-understanding-fibonacci-and-c.title: Check Your Understanding: Fibonacci and Call Trees

questions.question: Why does the call tree for `fib n` branch into two children at every non-base node, while the trace for `fac n` is a single chain?
options: Because `fib`'s recursive step calls `fib` twice — once for `n - 1` and once for `n - 2` — while `fac`'s recursive step calls `fac` only once
Because `fib` works on lists and `fac` works on numbers
Because `fib` has two base cases and `fac` has one
Because GHCi always draws Fibonacci calls as a tree for readability
questions.explanation: `fib n = fib (n - 1) + fib (n - 2)` makes two recursive calls per step, so each node in the trace has two children. `fac n = n * fac (n - 1)` makes only one recursive call per step, so its trace is a single chain. How many base cases a function has affects how many places the recursion can stop, not how many branches each step makes.
optionFeedback: Correct — two calls per step is exactly what turns a chain into a tree.
Both `fib` and `fac` have type `Integer -> Integer`; neither works on lists. The branching comes from how many times the function calls itself per step, not from the type it operates on.
It's true `fib` needs two base cases and `fac` needs one, but that's a separate fact — it explains how many places the recursion can *stop*, not how many children each non-base call produces.
GHCi does not draw anything automatically. The tree is a picture of how many calls happen, worked out by hand from the definition.

questions.question: In the `fib 5` tree, `fib 2` is evaluated three separate times. What does this tell you about the naive `fib` definition?
options: It recomputes the same sub-results from scratch every time they are needed, rather than reusing them
It has a bug that makes it loop forever on some inputs
`fib 2` is being memoized (cached) automatically by Haskell
The definition is wrong and gives incorrect answers for `n >= 5`
questions.explanation: Nothing in `fib`'s definition remembers a previously computed value. Each branch of the tree is evaluated completely independently, so identical sub-calls like `fib 2` are redone every time they occur. The answers are still correct — this is a performance concern, not a correctness one.
optionFeedback: Correct — no result is cached anywhere, so identical calls get redone from scratch.
`fib 5` terminates fine and returns the right answer, `5`. Repeated work is a performance concern, not a termination bug.
Plain Haskell functions are not memoized automatically. Nothing caches `fib 2`'s result between the three times it is called here.
The tree checked out against the Fibonacci table (`F5 = 5`), so the answer is correct. Repeated calls cost time, not correctness.

questions.question: Why is it fine that `isOdd` is defined after `isEven` in the source file, even though `isEven`'s body already refers to `isOdd`?
options: Top-level function definitions in a module are all visible to each other regardless of the order they are written in; only the equations *within* one function are tried in order
GHC secretly reorders the file so that `isOdd` is compiled before `isEven`
It only works because both functions happen to have a base case for `0`
It is not actually fine — this example only works because `isEven` happens to get called first with an even number
questions.explanation: The 'order matters' rule from earlier in this chapter applies to the equations of one function, matched top to bottom. It says nothing about the order in which two different top-level functions are written in a file — all top-level names are in scope for each other throughout the module, which is exactly what makes mutual recursion possible.
optionFeedback: Correct — the module is compiled as a whole, so both names are already visible everywhere in it.
GHC does not need to reorder anything; there is no hidden compilation pass that moves definitions around.

The base cases matter for termination, not for whether the definitions can reference each other. Two functions could reference each other with no base case at all and still compile — they just would not terminate.
Trace `isOdd 7` yourself: it hands off to `isEven 6`, `isOdd 5`, … down to `isEven 0`. It works regardless of which function is called first or whether the starting value is even or odd.

questions.question: Using the definitions above, what does `isOdd 4` evaluate to, and which base case does the chain of handoffs finally reach?
options: `False` — the chain ends at `isOdd 0`
`True` — the chain ends at `isEven 0`
`False` — the chain ends at `isEven 0`
`True` — the chain ends at `isOdd 0`
questions.explanation: `isOdd 4 = isEven 3 = isOdd 2 = isEven 1 = isOdd 0 = False`. Four handoffs bring the argument down to `0`, and because `isOdd 4` started the chain, it lands on `isOdd 0`, not `isEven 0`. `isOdd 0` is defined as `False`, matching the fact that `4` is not odd.
optionFeedback: Correct — four handoffs land on `isOdd 0`, which is `False`.
`isOdd 4` is `False`, not `True` — `4` is even, so it is not odd. Trace it: `isOdd 4 = isEven 3 = isOdd 2 = isEven 1 = isOdd 0`.
The value `False` is right, but check where the chain actually stops: `isOdd 4 = isEven 3 = isOdd 2 = isEven 1 = isOdd 0`. It is `isOdd 0` that fires, not `isEven 0`.
The chain does stop at `isOdd 0`, but `isOdd 0` is defined as `False`, not `True` — so `isOdd 4` is `False`, matching that `4` is not an odd number.
